articles.title: Meteorite that smashed through a New Jersey roof reveals clues to life’s origins
articles.summary: A rare meteorite that crashed through a New Jersey roof contains evidence of ancient salty fluids, organic compounds, and amino acids from a primitive asteroid. Its pristine chemistry could offer new clues about how space rocks helped supply early Earth with some of the ingredients needed for life.
articles.content:
A meteor streaked across the New York City area in broad daylight on July 16, 2024, producing a sonic boom as it passed just south of the Statue of Liberty. Not long afterward, a meteorite weighing more than two pounds punched through the roof of a home in Hillsborough, New Jersey. An international research team has now analyzed the recovered material and reported its findings in Science Advances.

"A forensic study of the fragments revealed that they contained preserved bits from near the surface of a primitive asteroid where it experienced concentrated salty fluids -- a process not previously known from this type of proto-planet world," said lead author and meteor astronomer Peter Jenniskens of the SETI Institute and NASA's Ames Research Center in California's Silicon Valley.

A Meteor Tracked Across the Northeast

The object that entered Earth's atmosphere that day was roughly the size of a heavy airline bag and was traveling at 32,000 miles/h (14.4 kilometers per second). Sixty people across New York, New Jersey, Connecticut, Rhode Island and Pennsylvania reported seeing the meteor to the American Meteor Society. Sixteen people in New York and New Jersey also reported feeling the shockwave.

"Our cameras in Northford, Connecticut, and Douglassville, Pennsylvania, as well as a doorbell camera in Wayne, New Jersey, captured the meteor, and from that we measured its trajectory," said American Meteor Society operations manager Mike Hankey. "The path traced back to low in the asteroid belt."

The incoming rock was fragile and broke apart quickly as it traveled through the atmosphere. It disappeared from view at an altitude of 22 miles (35 kilometers). Soon afterward, Doppler weather radar at Newark Airport briefly detected an elongated cloud of falling pebbles extending from Staten Island into New Jersey.

Hillsborough sat near the far end of that debris path, where the largest pieces were expected to reach the ground. Only one meteorite was recovered, largely because it made its presence impossible to miss by striking a house.

The homeowner recalled what happened: "I was at home at the time, heard a loud crash and found a hole in the ceiling of the master bedroom. I smelled a strong sulfur-like odor and saw many black fragments along with debris and black dust that covered my bed, carpet and surrounding areas."

He quickly documented the scene and protected the material from contamination. Wearing disposable gloves, he used aluminum foil to collect the meteorite fragments and placed them in glass jars.

An Exceptionally Rare Primitive Meteorite

Laboratory analysis showed that the recovered rock belonged to a primitive meteorite family known as CM-type carbonaceous chondrites. The "M" refers to the Mighei meteorite, which fell in Ukraine in 1889.

Paper coauthor Mike Zolensky, a meteoriticist at NASA's Johnson Space Center in Houston, found that some parts of the Hillsborough meteorite had experienced more extensive alteration by water on its parent asteroid than scientists usually observe in CM2 carbonaceous chondrites.

The meteorite was classified as a CM1/2 carbonaceous chondrite, placing it between the petrographic CM1 and CM2 categories.

The Hillsborough event is only the 22nd observed fall involving a CM-type meteorite. More remarkably, it is just the second witnessed fall of a CM1/2 carbonaceous chondrite. The first was the Kolang meteorite, which fell in North Sumatra, Indonesia, in 2020. Every other witnessed CM fall has involved CM2 material, and no CM1 meteorite fall has ever been observed.

"Thanks to the homeowner's quick reaction, these are the most pristine CM1/2 meteorites we know of," said Jenniskens.

Evidence of Ancient Asteroid Brines

Scientists are particularly interested in how water influenced the chemistry of primitive asteroids. Another major group of primitive carbonaceous chondrites is known as CI, with the "I" referring to the Ivuna meteorite that fell in Tanzania in 1938.

Pristine samples related to this type have also been returned directly from space. JAXA's Hayabusa 2 mission brought material back from asteroid Ryugu, while NASA's OSIRIS-REx mission returned samples from asteroid Bennu. Those samples contain substantial evidence that briny fluids once existed just beneath the surfaces of their parent asteroids.

Zolensky and colleague JangMi Han discovered small CM1 fragments rich in salt inside the Hillsborough meteorite. Their findings suggest that the material came from a region near the surface of its parent asteroid, where liquid water evaporated and left behind increasingly concentrated salts.

The researchers are now identifying the specific salt minerals in the meteorite so they can compare them with similar materials found in samples returned from Ryugu and Bennu.

This salty chemistry could have important implications for understanding the chemical conditions that helped produce molecules relevant to life. Highly concentrated brines can keep phosphate dissolved in solution and can promote chemical reactions involving organic compounds and minerals that precipitate from solution.

Organic Molecules and Ingredients for Life

"Isotope studies of carbon and nitrogen suggest that primitive carbonaceous chondrites, including CM-types, delivered organic matter to the early Earth," said cosmochemist Queenie Chan of Royal Holloway University of London, England, and biogeochemist Nana Ogawa of the Biogeochemistry Research Center at the Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology. "The Hillsborough meteorite contained 1.8% by weight of carbon and 0.07% of nitrogen, and had carbon and nitrogen isotopes typical for CM-type meteorites."

Researchers also detected a broad range of soluble organic compounds in the meteorite. The diversity of those compounds provides further evidence that the Hillsborough material experienced more extensive alteration by water than most other CM-type meteorites.

"A high fraction of compounds were the product of organic chemistry with minerals," said organic mass spectrometry specialist Phil Schmitt-Kopplin of Technical University Munich. "We do not know if these magnesium organic compounds were contributed by brine chemistry or were simply left over from earlier impact shock processes."

Organometallic compounds also play important roles in living systems, including in blood and photosynthesis. Scientists found numerous amino acids among the soluble organic compounds in the Hillsborough meteorite as well. They were similar to amino acids previously detected in CM2 chondrites that experienced more moderate water alteration.

Astrobiologist Danny Glavin of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, and researchers in Goddard's Astrobiology Analytical Lab concluded that CM-type bodies could have supplied the early Earth with amino acids, carboxylic acids and other soluble organic molecules. That delivery may have contributed to the collection of prebiotic organic material that existed before life emerged.

Their analysis also indicates that the meteorite's complex assortment of amino acids formed inside its parent body. Briny fluids likely helped drive at least some of that chemistry.

A Rare Asteroid Sample Preserved for Science

Some fragments of the Hillsborough meteorite will eventually be curated by the American Museum of Natural History in New York City, preserving the unusual material for future research.

"We are thrilled that nature delivered such a precious asteroid sample on our doorstep," said curator Denton Ebel.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a rare, scientifically significant meteorite fall that provides new, detailed insights into the chemistry of primitive asteroids and the origins of life on Earth. The discovery has broad implications for astrobiology and planetary science, offering tangible benefits to humanity's understanding of life's beginnings. The story is focused on a single event with substantial context and scientific analysis, demonstrating a meaningful positive impact on knowledge about space and life origins.
articles.personality_title: Rare meteorite in New Jersey offers new clues about life’s beginnings
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – On July 16, 2024, a meteor was seen flying across the skies near New York City and surrounding states. This space rock broke apart quickly but one large piece crashed through the roof of a home in Hillsborough, New Jersey. Scientists quickly collected the fragments to study them.

**What happened** – The meteorite weighs over two pounds and is from a rare type of space rock called a CM1/2 carbonaceous chondrite. This meteorite showed signs of salty water and organic molecules, including amino acids. These ingredients are important because they can help explain how life’s building blocks arrived on early Earth. Cameras and weather radar helped track the meteor’s path from the asteroid belt to the ground.

**Impact** – This meteorite is very special because only 22 falls of this kind have ever been seen, and this is just the second of its exact type. Its chemistry is very well preserved, showing salty fluids and complex organic compounds that formed inside its parent asteroid billions of years ago. Studying it helps scientists understand how space rocks might have delivered important materials that helped life begin on Earth.

**What's next step** – Parts of the meteorite will be kept at the American Museum of Natural History for future research. Scientists will continue studying the salt minerals and organic molecules to compare them with samples brought back from other asteroids by space missions. These studies will improve our knowledge of the conditions that allowed life’s ingredients to form in space.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A rare meteorite that fell in New Jersey reveals detailed evidence of ancient salty water and organic molecules, shedding light on how space rocks contributed to life’s origins on Earth.

articles.personality_title_es: Una rara meteorito en Nueva Jersey ofrece nuevas pistas sobre los orígenes de la vida
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – El 16 de julio de 2024, un meteorito cruzó el cielo cerca de Nueva York y estados vecinos. Esta roca espacial se rompió rápidamente, pero un pedazo grande atravesó el techo de una casa en Hillsborough, Nueva Jersey. Los científicos recogieron los fragmentos para estudiarlos.

**Qué pasó** – El meteorito pesa más de dos libras y pertenece a un tipo raro de roca espacial llamada condrita carbonácea CM1/2. Esta roca mostró señales de agua salada y moléculas orgánicas, incluyendo aminoácidos. Estos ingredientes son importantes porque ayudan a entender cómo llegaron los bloques básicos de la vida a la Tierra primitiva. Cámaras y radares meteorológicos siguieron su camino desde el cinturón de asteroides hasta el suelo.

**Impacto** – Este meteorito es muy especial porque solo se han visto 22 caídas de este tipo, y esta es solo la segunda de su tipo exacto. Su química está muy bien conservada, mostrando fluidos salados y compuestos orgánicos complejos formados dentro de su asteroide padre hace miles de millones de años. Estudiarlo ayuda a los científicos a saber cómo las rocas espaciales pudieron traer materiales importantes que ayudaron a la aparición de la vida en la Tierra.

**Próximo paso** – Algunas partes del meteorito serán guardadas en el Museo Americano de Historia Natural para futuras investigaciones. Los científicos seguirán estudiando los minerales salinos y las moléculas orgánicas para compararlos con muestras traídas de otros asteroides por misiones espaciales. Estos estudios mejorarán nuestro conocimiento sobre las condiciones que permitieron la formación de los ingredientes de la vida en el espacio.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Un meteorito raro que cayó en Nueva Jersey revela evidencia detallada de agua salada antigua y moléculas orgánicas, mostrando cómo las rocas espaciales contribuyeron a los orígenes de la vida en la Tierra.

articles.title: The sun is covered in tiny whirlpools we’ve never seen before
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered incredibly tiny plasma whirlpools swirling across the Sun’s surface, some just 20 kilometers wide. These previously invisible vortices may twist magnetic fields and help build up the energy released in small solar eruptions called nanoflares. They may also help magnetic fields spread through the Sun’s atmosphere far faster than current models can explain.
articles.content:
Scientists have captured previously unseen plasma vortices swirling across the surface of the Sun, revealing tiny structures that could help explain how our star stores, moves, and releases magnetic energy.

The discovery comes from researchers at the U.S. National Science Foundation National Solar Observatory (NSF NSO), the Max Planck Institute for Solar System Research (MPS) in Germany, and the High Altitude Observatory (HAO) in the USA. The team combined observations from the NSF Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope, the world's largest solar telescope, with advanced computer simulations. Built and operated by the NSO in Hawaii, the telescope provided images detailed enough to expose plasma motions that had never previously been visible.

"To detect the vortices, we needed to resolve structures on the solar surface about 20 kilometers in size. That is at the limit of what even the world's largest solar telescope and state-of-the-art simulations can achieve," said MPS scientist and co-author of the new publication Michiel van Noort, who contributed to the observations as well as the data reduction and image restoration. The researchers used a broadband imaging camera provided by the Max-Planck-Institute for Solar System Research (MPS).

Tiny Whirlpools Along Solar Granules

The newly detected vortices appear along the boundaries of structures known as granules, which densely cover the Sun's visible surface. Individual granules are typically between 500 and 2,000 kilometers across.

Together, they create the Sun's granulation, a constantly changing pattern that resembles bubbles in a boiling liquid. The comparison is fitting because granulation is produced by moving plasma. Hot plasma rises from deeper inside the Sun, cools near the surface, and then sinks back down.

For the first time, scientists were able to resolve extremely fine, fringe-like structures along the edges of these granules. The structures repeatedly develop swirling motions that resemble ocean waves as they begin to break.

Some of these "fringes" measure only slightly more than 20 kilometers across. Observing something that small on the Sun is roughly equivalent to identifying a one euro coin from 180 kilometers away.

Instabilities in the Solar Plasma

The researchers believe these swirling flows are evidence of Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities, a familiar phenomenon in fluid dynamics.

Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities develop when two fluids move alongside one another at different speeds. The difference in velocity produces shear forces where the two flows meet. Small disturbances at that boundary can then grow into waves or swirling vortices.

The same basic process appears in many environments and across vastly different scales -- for example, on the surfaces of lakes or in ocean waves, in cloud formation, in the atmospheres of the giant gas planets Jupiter and Saturn, and in the interaction of the solar wind with planetary magnetospheres.

At the boundaries of solar granules, neighboring layers of plasma also appear to travel at different speeds. Those conditions could provide exactly what is needed for Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities to form.

Tiny Vortices Could Twist Magnetic Fields

The newly observed plasma vortices may offer an important clue to how the Sun stores and releases energy within its magnetic field, including through tiny bursts of radiation called nanoflares.

Current theories suggest that magnetic energy builds up as the Sun's magnetic field lines become twisted and coiled -- similar to the mechanical energy stored in a tightly coiled metal spring. As the twisting increases, the magnetic configuration becomes both highly energetic and unstable.

Eventually, that stored energy can be released through a process known as "magnetic reconnection." During reconnection, twisted magnetic field lines snap open and reconnect in a different arrangement.

One major unanswered question has been what causes those magnetic field lines to become twisted in the first place.

The newly discovered vortices could supply part of the answer. Because the researchers find that these small whirlpools appear continuously wherever the magnetic field is sufficiently strong, the vortices could provide a persistent mechanism for twisting the Sun's magnetic field lines.

A Possible Clue to the Sun's Magnetic Cycle

The analysis also indicates that the mini-vortices are highly effective at mixing magnetized and non-magnetized plasma at the solar surface. That mixing could help magnetic fields move quickly from the surface upward into the Sun's atmosphere.

Changes in the Sun's magnetic field drive its roughly eleven-year activity cycle -- which is exceptionally rapid on a cosmic scale. For the Sun's magnetic "framework" to change this quickly, magnetic flux must be transported efficiently away through the solar atmosphere.

Current models have difficulty explaining how this diffusion can happen so rapidly. The newly identified vortices could provide an important piece of that puzzle as well.

"The newly discovered plasma vortices impressively demonstrate how minute processes -- at the limit of what we can resolve using all available techniques -- significantly determine the nature of our star," said Sami K. Solanki, director of the MPS and co-author of the new publication.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific discovery of tiny plasma whirlpools on the Sun's surface that help explain fundamental solar processes such as magnetic energy storage, nanoflares, and the Sun's magnetic cycle. This breakthrough advances understanding of solar physics with broad implications for space weather and astrophysics, representing a meaningful real-world impact and scientific progress.
articles.personality_title: Scientists discover tiny whirlpools on the Sun that may explain solar energy bursts
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists have long studied the Sun’s surface to understand how it stores and releases magnetic energy. The Sun’s surface is covered with granules, which are bubbling patterns caused by hot plasma moving up and down.

**What happened** – Researchers from the U.S. and Germany used the world’s largest solar telescope in Hawaii and computer simulations to spot tiny whirlpools, or vortices, just 20 kilometers wide on the Sun’s surface. These whirlpools form along the edges of granules and were detected for the first time thanks to powerful imaging tools.

**Impact** – These small whirlpools may twist the Sun’s magnetic fields, helping build up energy that causes tiny solar explosions called nanoflares. They also might explain how magnetic fields move quickly through the Sun’s atmosphere, which is important for understanding the Sun’s 11-year activity cycle. This discovery fills a gap in how scientists explain solar energy changes and magnetic field behavior.

**What's next step** – Scientists will continue studying these whirlpools to learn exactly how they affect magnetic fields and energy release. This could improve predictions of solar activity and help us understand space weather that affects Earth.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Tiny plasma whirlpools discovered on the Sun’s surface reveal new details about how the star stores and releases magnetic energy.
articles.personality_title_fr: Des scientifiques découvrent de minuscules tourbillons sur le Soleil qui pourraient expliquer les explosions d’énergie solaire
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les scientifiques étudient depuis longtemps la surface du Soleil pour comprendre comment il stocke et libère l’énergie magnétique. La surface du Soleil est recouverte de granules, des motifs bouillonnants causés par le mouvement du plasma chaud.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des chercheurs des États-Unis et d’Allemagne ont utilisé le plus grand télescope solaire du monde à Hawaï et des simulations informatiques pour repérer de minuscules tourbillons, ou vortex, d’à peine 20 kilomètres de large à la surface du Soleil. Ces tourbillons apparaissent le long des bords des granules et ont été détectés pour la première fois grâce à des outils d’imagerie puissants.

**Impact** – Ces petits tourbillons pourraient tordre les champs magnétiques du Soleil, aidant à accumuler l’énergie qui provoque de petites explosions solaires appelées nanoflares. Ils pourraient aussi expliquer comment les champs magnétiques se déplacent rapidement dans l’atmosphère solaire, ce qui est important pour comprendre le cycle d’activité de 11 ans du Soleil. Cette découverte comble une lacune dans la compréhension des changements d’énergie solaire et du comportement des champs magnétiques.

**Prochaine étape** – Les scientifiques vont continuer à étudier ces tourbillons pour comprendre précisément comment ils influencent les champs magnétiques et la libération d’énergie. Cela pourrait améliorer la prévision de l’activité solaire et notre compréhension du climat spatial qui affecte la Terre.

**Résumé en une phrase** – De minuscules tourbillons de plasma découverts à la surface du Soleil révèlent de nouveaux détails sur la façon dont notre étoile stocke et libère son énergie magnétique.
articles.personality_title_es: Científicos descubren diminutos remolinos en el Sol que podrían explicar las explosiones de energía solar
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los científicos han estudiado durante mucho tiempo la superficie del Sol para entender cómo almacena y libera energía magnética. La superficie del Sol está cubierta de gránulos, patrones burbujeantes causados por el movimiento del plasma caliente.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores de Estados Unidos y Alemania usaron el telescopio solar más grande del mundo en Hawái y simulaciones por computadora para detectar pequeños remolinos, o vórtices, de solo 20 kilómetros de ancho en la superficie del Sol. Estos remolinos aparecen a lo largo de los bordes de los gránulos y fueron detectados por primera vez gracias a herramientas de imagen muy avanzadas.

**Impacto** – Estos pequeños remolinos pueden torcer los campos magnéticos del Sol, ayudando a acumular energía que causa pequeñas explosiones solares llamadas nanoflares. También podrían explicar cómo los campos magnéticos se mueven rápidamente a través de la atmósfera solar, lo que es importante para entender el ciclo de actividad de 11 años del Sol. Este descubrimiento llena un vacío en la explicación de los cambios de energía solar y el comportamiento de los campos magnéticos.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos seguirán estudiando estos remolinos para aprender exactamente cómo afectan los campos magnéticos y la liberación de energía. Esto podría mejorar la predicción de la actividad solar y ayudarnos a entender el clima espacial que afecta a la Tierra.

**Resumen en una frase** – Pequeños remolinos de plasma descubiertos en la superficie del Sol revelan nuevos detalles sobre cómo la estrella almacena y libera energía magnética.
